papers.title: Onset of subdiffusion in dephased quasiperiodic lattices
papers.abstract: Dephasing is widely expected to induce diffusion in quasiperiodic lattices due to the loss of phase coherence. However, this expectation can fail dramatically in lattices possessing singular onsite potentials or vanishing hoppings which are expected to trivially localize the particle. Remarkably, we show that the transport in such lattices can be subdiffusive under proper conditions for which the "mean resistance" of the lattice diverges. As a result, we obtain a transition from diffusive to subdiffusive transport depending on the strength of quasiperiodic modulation. Even more strikingly, the transport is slowest not deep in the subdiffusive regime but precisely at its onset, forming a sharp "subdiffusive trench". Our analytical and numerical analysis reveal that the transport exponents are universal, fixed solely by the order of singularities (zeros) of the diagonal (off-diagonal) quasiperiodic modulation. In the end, we complement our findings through exact Lindblad simulations and provide possible experimental routes to realize such non-trivial transport.

papers.title: Geometric formulation of the orbital magnetic susceptibility of periodic insulators
papers.abstract: A gauge-invariant projector-based expression for the orbital magnetic susceptibility of periodic insulators is obtained from a density-matrix perturbation expansion in a uniform magnetic field. It is shown that, within such an approach, it is natural to distinguish two contributions: the Van Vleck paramagnetic contribution and a geometric contribution. The latter can be expressed in terms of fundamental geometric quantities built from projector derivatives such as the curvature and metric operators, as well as the closely related magnetic moment operator. When applied to two-band and four-band models, the expression for the susceptibility reduces to a simplified formula expressed in terms of the quantum metric. The significance of quantum geometry for the orbital magnetic response is then examined within a lattice model in two dimensions describing the transition between two distinct insulators via a Dirac semimetallic phase.

papers.title: Local-channel inequivalence within analytic symmetry-broken phases
papers.abstract: Gibbs states at different temperatures can be inequivalent under two-way quasi-local channels even within a single phase with spontaneously broken continuous symmetry and analytic free energy. We prove this for the symmetry-invariant Gibbs states of a canonical ideal Bose gas at fixed density and a classical vortex-free Villain model on hypercubic lattices in $d\ge3$ dimensions. At lower temperatures, two distant observers can estimate the shared direction of order more accurately. The maximum mutual information they can obtain by separate measurements grows logarithmically with the radius of their regions. The leading term is the same throughout each ordered phase, while the constant term $\mathcal{C}(T)=\tfrac12\ln[\Upsilon(T)/T]+c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is strictly larger at lower temperatures. Here $\Upsilon(T)$ is the phase stiffness and $c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ depends only on the region geometry. A quasi-local channel cannot increase this constant, so it is invariant under two-way conversion. Cooling would increase it and is therefore impossible between any two distinct temperatures in the ordered phase. On finite lattices, cooling with vanishing error requires a circuit whose causal radius grows at least linearly with the lattice side length. We also obtain the invariant for quantum and multicomponent Villain models and conjecture a stiffness formula for more general patterns of continuous symmetry breaking.

papers.title: Quadratic Models for Engineered Control of Open Quantum Systems
papers.abstract: We introduce a framework to model the evolution of a class of open quantum systems whose environments periodically undergo an instantaneous non-unitary evolution stage. For the special case of quadratic models, we show how this approach can generalise the formalism of repeated interactions to allow for the preservation of system-environment correlations. Furthermore, its continuous zero-period limit provides a natural description of the evolution of small systems coupled to large environments in negligibly perturbed steady states. We explore the advantages and limitations of this approach in illustrative applications to thermalisation in a simple hopping ring and to the problem of initialising a qubit chain via environmental engineering.

papers.title: Simulating and Sampling from Quantum Circuits with 2D Tensor Networks
papers.abstract: Classical simulations of quantum circuits play a vital role in the development of quantum computers and for taking the temperature of the field. Here, we classically simulate various physically-motivated circuits using 2D tensor network ans\"atze for the many-body wavefunction which match the geometry of the underlying quantum processor. We then employ a generalized version of the boundary Matrix Product State contraction algorithm to controllably generate samples from the resultant tensor network states. Our approach allows us to systematically converge both the quality of the final state and the samples drawn from it to the true distribution defined by the circuit, with GPU hardware providing us with significant speedups over CPU hardware. With these methods, we simulate the largest local unitary Jastrow ansatz circuit taken from recent IBM experiments to numerical precision. We also study a domain-wall quench in a two-dimensional discrete-time Heisenberg model on large heavy-hex and rotated square lattices, which reflect IBM's and Google's latest quantum processors respectively. We observe a rapid buildup of complex loop correlations on the Google Willow geometry which significantly impact the local properties of the system. Meanwhile, we find loop correlations build up extremely slowly on heavy-hex processors and have almost negligible impact on the local properties of the system, even at large circuit depths. Our results underscore the role the geometry of the quantum processor plays in classical simulability.

papers.title: Projected evolution of quantum gates for circuit simulation with matrix product states
papers.abstract: Tensor networks and specifically matrix product states (MPS) enable feasible classical quantum circuit simulation when entanglement remains compressible, but for this, gate updates must balance accuracy, representation size, and runtime. Conventional methods incorporate a complete gate into the MPS before compressing enlarged bonds. Here, we instead use lessons from the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) to analyze the projected action of each gate on the MPS by reducing it to a continuous generator path. We establish the spatial and state-space structure of this projected evolution and show that both the fixed-rank and two-site actions are confined to a contiguous window spanned by the gate while retaining boundary information from the surrounding MPS. Within this window characterization, we delineate when the instantaneous two-site action is exact and when variational directions can block it completely. Using standard nearest-point-projection geometry, we also show that fixed-rank TDVP and the local nearest fixed-rank projection of the exact gate endpoint agree to first order. We implement the gate-window restriction with rank-adaptive two-site TDVP and test both the projected update and a hybrid method that reserves it for long-range gates. Across the circuit benchmarks, these implementations incur runtime overhead and show no consistent accuracy--cost advantage over the tested baseline methods. The resulting framework provides a gate-specific structural analysis and a tested implementation together with explicit limits on its practical performance.

papers.title: Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations
papers.abstract: Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistors (GAAFETs) are emerging as successors to Fin Field-Effect Transistors (FinFETs) and are central to continued scaling at advanced semiconductor nodes. Despite their improved electrostatic control, recent measurements show that the drain current in GAAFETs deviates strongly from thermionic behavior at negative gate voltages, increasing as the gate voltage becomes more negative. This leakage has been attributed to direct gate-drain tunneling through the high-$k$ dielectric, enhanced by drain-induced dielectric barrier lowering (DIDBL). Here, we use predictive, charge-self-consistent Non-Equilibrium Green Function (NEGF) simulations based on the Contact Block Reduction (CBR) method to spatially resolve this leakage pathway in GAAFETs. Unlike approaches based primarily on phenomenological leakage models, our first-principles, multi-terminal quantum-transport framework treats the source, drain, and gate as current-carrying quantum-mechanical contacts and resolves the local current density throughout the device. The spatially resolved current density shows that gate-injected carriers tunnel through the high-$k$ dielectric preferentially near the drain side of the gate, where the dielectric barrier is most strongly lowered by the drain bias, and are collected by the drain. This provides a direct real-space picture of the DIDBL-driven gate-drain leakage mechanism.

papers.title: The often overlooked role of sound in liquid thermal transport
papers.abstract: Formulated a hundred years ago, the Bridgman formula for thermal conductivity of liquids postulates a proportionality between sound velocity and thermal conductivity. This designates phonons as heat carriers in a liquid. Its empirical success has been under-appreciated and its conceptual implications overlooked. Here, we review its origin, its links to hydrodynamic Euler equations and to the fundamental paradox surrounding the parabolic heat equation and its fate across the quantum-classical crossover.

papers.title: Dopant depth determination from momentum-resolved core-loss 4D-STEM data
papers.abstract: Moving beyond specimen-projected micrographs in scanning transmission electron microscopy to determine a three-dimensional distribution of dopants is of vital importance for materials characterization and development. Within the Born approximation, Fourier transformation over probe position of a momentum-resolved core-loss 4D-STEM dataset reveals fringes whose frequency encodes the dopant's distance from the focal plane. We address two principal challenges which arise under experimental circumstances. First, fringe contrast is degraded by dynamical scattering, but can be partially recovered by acquiring off major zone axes. Second, the excessive doses typical of core-loss scattering can be alleviated using a Bayesian framework which, on a simulated Fe-doped strontium titanate, achieves nanometre to sub-nanometre depth precision from 100 to 1000 core-loss counts, depending on the signal-to-background.
